issues.legal_issue: A mining lease is granted when an agreement fixes its terms and gives the lessee present possession, even if a formal lease deed is executed later.
material_facts: An agreement fixing the terms of a perpetual lease was made in 1939, and possession was delivered under it.
The agreement described the transaction as a lease, set out its terms, and was acted upon by the parties.
A formal lease deed was executed in 1951 following a decree for specific performance of the agreement.
issues.conclusion: The lease was granted when the agreement was made, not when the formal deed was executed, and therefore qualified as an existing mining lease under the 1956 Rules.
issues.legal_principle: The grant of a lease is distinct from formal execution of its deed; execution may simply satisfy legal requirements for enforceability. Rule 28A of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, treats sanctioning as the grant and formal execution as a subsequent requirement. The parties’ agreement, which fixed the terms and was acted upon, itself effected the grant.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_mining_lease_modification and agreement_fixed_lease_terms and possession_delivered_under_agreement and formal_deed_executed_later

predicates.appeal_challenging_mining_lease_modifica: A party appealed an order modifying the terms of a mining lease.
predicates.agreement_fixed_lease_terms: The parties made an agreement that set out the terms of the mining lease.
predicates.possession_delivered_under_agreement: The lessor delivered possession to the lessee under the agreement.
predicates.formal_deed_executed_later: The parties executed a formal lease deed after making and acting on the agreement.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges modification of a mining lease, an agreement that fixed the lease terms and was followed by delivery of possession is treated as the grant even if a formal deed came later.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for laws modifying mineral rights applies to leases for extracting minerals and related purposes, not only to the initial preparation of a mine for working.
material_facts: The lease authorized excavation of white clay and its removal from the leased land.
The challenged rules modified the lease, including its duration and royalty terms.
The appellant argued that the lease covered extraction and removal, not merely the narrow process of making a mine workable.
issues.conclusion: The lease was for winning minerals within Article 31A(1)(e), so the modification rules were not invalid on the ground that they abridged rights under Articles 14, 19 or 31.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(e) uses “winning” broadly to mean getting or extracting minerals from mines and purposes incidental to that activity. Definitions of “winning” or “win” in statutes and rules are framed for their own limited purposes and do not control the meaning of the constitutional provision. The court distinguished the narrow, lease-specific usage in Lewis v. Fothergill and Lord Rokeby v. Elliot.

predicates.appeal_challenging_mining_lease_modifica: A party appealed an order modifying the terms of a mining lease.
predicates.lease_authorized_mineral_extraction: The lease authorized the lessee to extract minerals from the leased area.
predicates.modification_related_to_mining_rights: The challenged modification governed rights connected with extracting minerals or related mining activity.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges a modification of a lease authorizing mineral extraction and the modification concerns mining rights, the modification is protected from the stated fundamental-rights challenge.

issues.legal_issue: Rules regulating mines and mineral development were within the Central Legislature’s competence and were not rules for acquisition or requisition of property.
material_facts: The 1956 Rules regulated modification of mining leases in connection with the regulation of mines and development of minerals.
The Rules were made before the 1956 constitutional amendment that changed the legislative entries concerning acquisition and requisition of property.
The appellant argued that the Rules were beyond the Central Legislature’s competence before that amendment.
issues.conclusion: The Rules were within the Central Legislature’s competence because they concerned regulation of mines and development of minerals, not acquisition or requisition of property.
issues.legal_principle: The relevant legislative competence arose from the Union’s power over regulation of mines and mineral development to the extent declared expedient in the public interest. The court held that the Rules fell within that field, rather than the then-existing legislative entries concerning acquisition and requisition of property.

predicates.appeal_challenging_mining_lease_modifica: A party appealed an order modifying the terms of a mining lease.
predicates.rules_regulated_mines_or_mineral_develop: The challenged rules governed the regulation of mines or the development of minerals.
predicates.rules_did_not_provide_for_property_acqui: The rules regulated mining rights rather than providing for acquisition or requisition of property.

issues.definition: In an appeal challenging mining-lease modifications, rules regulating mines or mineral development, rather than property acquisition, are within Central legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: Rules made or purportedly made under an earlier mining statute can continue under a later mining statute when they concern matters provided for by the later statute and are not inconsistent with it.
material_facts: The 1956 Rules were made or purportedly made under the 1948 Act.
The later 1957 Act provided for the relevant subject matter and included a provision continuing qualifying earlier rules.
The appellant argued that any invalidity under the 1948 Act prevented the Rules from continuing under the 1957 Act.
issues.conclusion: Even if the Rules were inconsistent with the 1948 Act, they could continue under the 1957 Act because they were deemed to have been made under it, subject to its terms.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 of the 1957 Act deems rules made or purportedly made under the 1948 Act, concerning matters provided for in the 1957 Act and not inconsistent with it, to have been made under the 1957 Act and to continue until superseded. Applying Abdul Majid v. P.R. Nayak, the court treated the later Act as having been in force when the earlier rules were made for purposes of their legal status under the later Act.

predicates.appeal_challenging_mining_lease_modifica: A party appealed an order modifying the terms of a mining lease.
predicates.earlier_rules_made_or_purportedly_made_u: The rules had been made or purportedly made under an earlier law governing mines and minerals.
predicates.later_law_provided_for_their_subject: A later law provided for the subject matter addressed by the earlier rules.
predicates.earlier_rules_not_inconsistent_with_late: The earlier rules were not inconsistent with the later law.

issues.definition: Earlier rules continue under a later law when the later law covers their subject and the rules do not conflict with it.

issues.legal_issue: The Controller may modify an existing mining lease to bring its terms into conformity with the later mining statute and rules made under it.
material_facts: The Controller modified the lease under the 1956 Rules, which continued under the 1957 Act.
The modifications addressed the lease’s duration, renewal, dead rent, royalty and application of statutory rules.
The Controller’s order was challenged on the ground that the Controller lacked authority to make the modifications.
issues.conclusion: The Controller was competent to modify the lease to bring it into conformity with the 1957 Act and the rules made under it.
issues.legal_principle: The 1956 Rules continued under section 29 of the 1957 Act, and the Controller could exercise the modification authority under those Rules to align existing leases with the 1957 Act and rules made under section 13. Section 7(2) of the 1948 Act and rules 6 and 7 of the 1956 Rules formed part of the relevant modification scheme.

predicates.appeal_challenging_mining_lease_modifica: A party appealed an order modifying the terms of a mining lease.
predicates.controller_modified_existing_lease_under: The Controller modified an existing lease using rules that continued to operate under the later mining law.
predicates.modification_aligned_lease_with_current_: The modification brought the lease terms into conformity with the current mining law and rules.

issues.definition: When the Controller uses continuing rules to align an existing lease with current mining law, the Controller’s authority to modify the lease is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: The duration of an existing mining lease modified to conform with a new statutory maximum is calculated from the commencement of the new regime, rather than from the original grant.
material_facts: The lease was originally perpetual and concerned extraction of white clay.
The 1957 Act limited the duration of a mining lease for that mineral to twenty years.
The Controller had counted the modified term from the original agreement, while the appellant sought a term beginning when the 1957 Act came into force.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the lease term was to run for twenty years from June 1, 1958, when the 1957 Act came into force, with renewal regulated by the law and rules in force when renewal fell due. Two judges dissented, reasoning that the term could be cut down from the original grant and that the appellant had no grievance against the Controller’s order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(1) of the 1957 Act limited the duration for which the relevant kind of mining lease could be granted. The majority reasoned that the Act regulated mining after its commencement and that an existing lease should be modified to permit the maximum term available for a new lease after that commencement. The dissent considered the original lease the subsisting lease and would have counted the reduced term from its grant.

predicates.appeal_challenging_duration_of_existing_: A party appealed a decision modifying the duration of an existing mining lease.
predicates.existing_lease_exceeded_new_statutory_ma: The existing lease’s duration exceeded the maximum permitted for a lease under the later mining regime.
predicates.modification_brought_lease_under_new_reg: The modification was intended to make the existing lease conform to the later mining regime.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an existing lease that exceeds the later regime’s maximum and the modification brings it into conformity, the modified term runs from the commencement of that regime.
